titleText.es: Vivimos en un mundo donde hay verdaderas flotas de robots asesinos patrullando los cielos. En algún momento dejamos el presente y nos metimos en el futuro.
titleText.en: We live in a world where there are actual fleets of robot assassins patrolling the skies. At some point there, we left the present and entered the future.
titleText.noteEn: The Spanish text is the exact title attribute in the Spanish archive, and the English text is the exact official xkcd title attribute.

regions.labelEs: ¡SARAH! ¡VEN CONMIGO SI QUIERES VIVIR! ¡HAN ENVIADO A UN ROBOT ASESINO PARA MATARTE!

excludedUnits.rationale: SARAH is a personal name identifying the film character, not Spanish vocabulary.

applications.explanationEn: Ven is the irregular positive command used to tell one familiar person to come.
Quieres matches one familiar listener, and vivir stays in its unchanged dictionary form as the desired action.
Han is the present helper for a plural sender, and enviado is enviar's completed-action form.
A marks the person-like robot as the direct recipient of the sending action, and the following noun phrase identifies that agent.
Asesino follows robot to classify it as a robot designed to kill.
Asesino uses masculine singular -o to match the masculine singular noun robot.
Para introduces the robot's purpose, and matar stays in its unchanged dictionary form inside matarte.
Te attaches to the end of the dictionary form matar and identifies the familiar listener as the person affected.

regions.labelEs: ESTOY AQUÍ PARA SALVARTE. PUEDE QUE NO SEA TAN FUERTE Y RÁPIDO COMO UNA MÁQUINA, PERO LUCHARÉ PARA...

applications.explanationEn: Estoy is a form of estar because the speaker is stating his location rather than his identity.
Para introduces the reason for being here, and salvar stays in its unchanged dictionary form inside salvarte.
Te attaches to the dictionary form salvar and identifies the familiar listener as the person being saved.
Puede que presents the description as possible rather than certain, and ser changes to the possibility form sea; no negates that form.
Tan sets the degree of the coordinated descriptions fuerte y rápido, and como introduces the comparison point.
Lucharé keeps the full verb luchar and adds the speaker's future ending -é.

cards.noteEn: Ven is the irregular positive command of venir, ‘to come,’ for tú, the familiar singular ‘you.’

cards.promptEs: orden afirmativa para tú: habla, come, escribe
cards.questionEn: How do you give one friend or familiar person a positive command?
cards.answerEn: Use the informal singular command form, often the same form used for “he” or “she” in the present.
cards.noteEn: For many regular verbs, -ar becomes -a and -er or -ir becomes -e: hablar becomes habla, comer becomes come, and escribir becomes escribe. Some common verbs are irregular or change their stem. Negative commands use a different form and are a separate pattern.

cards.promptEs: VEN CONMIGO SI QUIERES VIVIR · ROBOT ASESINO · BOOM
cards.answerEn: a Terminator-style rescue interrupted by the kind of robot attack the story imagines
cards.noteEn: Calling to Sarah with the famous rescue line signals the Terminator films. The would-be protector then faces an airborne robot assassin and is immediately interrupted by an explosion. The title, More Accurate, contrasts the heroic movie setup with a world where remote robotic weapons already exist.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what someone wants to do?
cards.answerEn: Use a form of querer, then the action verb in its unchanged dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged verb ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. Querer changes to match the person and time, while the desired action stays unchanged: quiero salir, quieres comer, queremos dormir. Spanish does not insert a between the two verbs.

cards.answerEn: Use he, has, ha, hemos, habéis, or han followed by the verb’s completed-action form.
cards.noteEn: These are forms of haber, the helper verb used here like English “have.” For most verbs, the completed-action form ends in -ado after an -ar verb and -ido after an -er or -ir verb. This form is called the past participle, and it does not change after haber. How often this tense is used instead of the simple past varies by region.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “have done,” as in “I have finished”?

cards.noteEn: Enviado is the completed-action form of enviar. After han, it says that more than one person or thing has sent something or someone.

example.es: Han enviado el paquete esta mañana.
example.en: They sent the package this morning.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; marks a person-denoting object
cards.noteEn: The personal a also appears before words such as alguien (“someone”) and nadie (“nobody”) when they directly receive an action, even though they do not identify one specific individual.

cards.promptEs: a + persona o expresión que se refiere a una persona
cards.questionEn: Why does Spanish sometimes put a before the person affected by an action?
cards.answerEn: Put a before a person—or a word such as alguien or nadie—when that person directly receives the action.
cards.noteEn: This a is called the personal a. It is common before a named or specific person, but person-denoting words such as alguien (“someone”) and nadie (“nobody”) also take it. English usually has no separate word for it. Before the masculine article el, a + el contracts to al.

cards.questionEn: Where does a basic Spanish describing word usually go relative to its noun?
cards.answerEn: Put it after the noun in the common neutral order.
cards.noteEn: Many ordinary descriptive words follow the person or thing they describe: un coche rojo, una casa grande. Some adjectives commonly come before the noun, and moving an adjective can change emphasis or meaning, so this is a useful default rather than an absolute rule.

cards.promptEs: adjetivo que concuerda con masculino o femenino
cards.questionEn: How does a Spanish describing word change for a man, woman, or gendered noun?
cards.answerEn: Make the describing word match the gender and number of the person or thing it describes.
cards.noteEn: Many describing words ending in -o change to -a for a feminine singular person or noun: cansado becomes cansada. Plurals normally add -s. Some describing words have one form for both genders.

example.es: Pedro está cansado y Ana está cansada.
example.en: Pedro is tired and Ana is tired.

cards.noteEn: After a masculine singular noun, asesino can describe something designed or used to kill. As a noun, asesino can also mean a male killer.

example.es: La novela presenta un virus asesino.
example.en: The novel features a killer virus.

cards.answerEn: Use para followed by the verb’s dictionary form.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form ends in -ar, -er, or -ir and is called the infinitive. Use para + verb when the same person or thing performs both actions: in estudio para aprender, I both study and learn. When someone else performs the second action, Spanish needs the different pattern para que.
cards.questionEn: How do you say “in order to do something” in Spanish?

example.en: I study in order to learn.

cards.noteEn: Matar stays in its unchanged dictionary form, and te attaches to its end for the person affected.

cards.promptEs: verbo en forma de diccionario + pronombre unido
cards.questionEn: Where can a short object word such as me, te, lo, or la go with an unchanged action verb?
cards.answerEn: Attach it to the end of the verb and write the result as one word.
cards.noteEn: An unchanged dictionary-form verb ends in -ar, -er, or -ir. Short object words can attach directly: conocer + te becomes conocerte, and ayudar + me becomes ayudarme.
Spanish uses a form of estar, rather than ser, to say where someone or something is. Estoy is the form for the speaker.

cards.promptEs: ser para identidad · estar para ubicación
cards.questionEn: Which Spanish “to be” verb says what something is, and which says where it is?
cards.answerEn: Use ser for identity or a defining description; use estar for the location of a person or thing.
cards.noteEn: This contrast is not simply permanent versus temporary. Forms of ser such as soy and es identify or describe what something is. Forms of estar such as están normally locate people and things. Events are a common exception: Spanish uses ser to say where or when an event takes place.

example.es: El museo es famoso y está en Madrid.
example.en: The museum is famous and is in Madrid.

cards.noteEn: Salvar stays in its unchanged dictionary form, and te attaches to its end for the person being saved.

example.en: The life jacket can save you.

cards.answerEn: may; might (as part of puede que)

cards.questionEn: How do you say that something may or might be true or happen?
cards.answerEn: Use puede que, then put the following verb in a special possibility form.
cards.noteEn: The special form is called the subjunctive: it presents the following idea as possible rather than as a plain fact. Puede que stays fixed, while the next verb changes to match its own subject; for example, llega becomes llegue and es becomes sea.

cards.answerEn: no separate English word; completes puede que (“may; might”)
is; may be (a possibility form of ser)
cards.noteEn: Sea is a form of ser used when something is presented as uncertain, possible, desired, or otherwise not stated as a plain fact. For a straightforward statement, the corresponding form is es.

cards.answerEn: as (before a description in tan… como)

cards.questionEn: How do you say that two things are equally strong in some quality?
cards.answerEn: Put tan before the describing word and como before the comparison: tan… como means “as… as.”
cards.noteEn: A describing word can describe a thing, such as claro (“clear”), or how an action happens, such as rápido (“quickly”). Tan and como stay unchanged; only the surrounding words change as the surrounding grammar requires.

example.es: El café está tan frío como el agua.
example.en: The coffee is as cold as the water.

cards.noteEn: Fuerte has the same singular form for masculine and feminine nouns; its plural is fuertes.
Unaccented como can introduce the person, thing, or situation used for a comparison. It does not ask “how”; the question word cómo has an accent.

cards.answerEn: I will fight; I will struggle
cards.noteEn: Lucharé keeps the full verb luchar and adds -é for a future action by the speaker.

example.en: I will fight for a fair solution.

cards.questionEn: How do you say what someone will do in Spanish?
cards.answerEn: Keep the action verb in its dictionary form and add a future ending such as -é, -ás, -á, -emos, -éis, or -án.
cards.noteEn: The dictionary form is the unchanged form ending in -ar, -er, or -ir. The ending identifies the person: sentir plus -á gives sentirá, and ver plus -á gives verá. A few common verbs change their stem, but use the same endings.

cards.answerEn: boom; the sound of an explosion
cards.noteEn: This comic keeps the internationally familiar English-style spelling BOOM as a printed sound effect. Spanish also commonly writes the sound as bum.

example.en: Boom! The box fell to the floor.
